sentences: The room is full of children, and full of noise.
One laughs, one cries, others sing at the top of their voices.
This is The Feast of Saint Nicholas, painted by the Dutch artist Jan Steen around 1665 to 1668.
In the Netherlands, people said that on the night of the fifth of December, the eve of his feast, Saint Nicholas left a present for every good child.
Children set out a shoe before they went to bed, and in the morning they rushed to see what was inside.
The custom is one of the roots of today's Santa Claus.
Jan Steen was born in Leiden around 1626.
Besides painting, he ran a brewery for a time and later kept an inn.
No one was better at turning the noisy, ordinary life of a household into a picture full of humour and small stories.
Look first at the little girl in the middle.
In one arm she holds a doll, and in her other hand a small bucket full of sweets.
Her mother opens her arms to her, but the girl clutches her presents tightly and will not let them go.
Now look at the boy on the left, who is in tears.
In his shoe there is no present at all, only a birch rod, the thing a naughty child was said to receive.
Another child holds the shoe up for everyone to see, and grins.
But look further back.
An old woman, his grandmother, beckons to him from beside the curtains of the bed.
Her gesture is usually read as a sign that his real present is hidden there.
His tears are about to turn to laughter.
On the right, a boy holding a baby points up the chimney, showing the way Saint Nicholas came and went in the night.
Beside him, other children tilt their heads back and sing, perhaps one of the old songs for the saint.
The floor and table are crowded with festive food: biscuits and nuts, gingerbread figures and a long, special loaf baked for the holiday.
Steen paints each treat with such care that you feel you are standing at the feast yourself.
Notice how every child's face has its own expression: delight, mischief, disappointment and wonder.
Steen loved to layer several small stories into a single room, so that the longer you look, the more you find.
Each figure seems to have its own part to play in the drama of the evening.
Steen was a Catholic.
In the strongly Protestant Dutch Republic of his day, the feast of a saint was often frowned upon by the authorities, yet families went on celebrating it at home, just as this one does.
Step back and see the whole room at once: joy, disappointment and hope, all under one roof.
This winter, what do you imagine you might find waiting in your own shoe?
